name: Applied Computer Science
overview: The first year moves through Python and databases, C programming with networks and hardware, cybersecurity, and then data science, cloud computing and responsible AI. After year one you pick embedded software development or cybersecurity. Learning is hands-on, with lab work, company-based projects and continuous assessment in place of big exams. Year two includes a minor or work placement, and year three brings a research project and a graduation thesis. Graduates work as IoT developers, cybersecurity analysts, cloud architects or software developers, or continue to a master's in applied or technical universities.

name: Electrical and Electronic Engineering
overview: Year one covers digital systems, electricity, magnetism, energy, drive systems and programming, alongside mathematics and physics. In year two you go deeper into embedded systems, energy technology and electronics through semester-long projects such as offshore wind turbine designs. Teaching mixes lectures, practicals in small groups and project teams of two to six students working on fictional cases or real company assignments. In year three you choose an internship or a minor in robotics, entrepreneurship or energy transition, then finish with a six-month graduation project at a company. Typical jobs include embedded systems, electronics design, control and test engineering.

name: European Studies
overview: Year one introduces Europe's institutions, law, politics, business and intercultural communication, alongside a modern language of your choice. Later years turn to sustainability in Europe, then peace, security and prosperity, and finally diversity in Europe. Work is project-based, with assignments such as policy advice, marketing plans and strategy documents rather than mainly exams. You spend five months on an exchange abroad, can add a minor, and in the final year complete a capstone project, a five-month internship and a graduation research project. Graduates become policy officers, sustainability advisors, lobbyists, export managers or communications professionals, and many go on to a master's.

name: Industrial Design Engineering
overview: The first year is built around integrated design projects, with courses in sketching, prototyping, studio work, user research, business planning and design software. Teaching is learning by doing: roughly 45 percent of the curriculum is project work, supported by workshops, a 3D protolab and laser cutters. Group projects for real clients such as Bosch, Ahrend and Rabobank are shown at end-of-semester design expos. In year three you take a minor, for example Design with Nature or Packaging Design and Innovation, or do an internship or exchange, then complete a graduation project for an external client. Graduates work as product, service or interaction designers, user researchers and innovation managers.

name: International and European Law
overview: You start with introductions to law, international law, private law and EU law, learning to write, reason and negotiate like a lawyer. Later years add international criminal law and corporate and trade law, and in year three you pick four electives such as corporate governance or climate and natural resources. Teaching leans on professional scenarios and moot court, where students argue for fictional clients, and many enter international moot competitions. You can take a minor or a semester abroad, and the fourth year combines an internship of at least 100 working days with an applied research project. Graduates become corporate lawyers, compliance officers, EU policy advisors or legal advisers in government, or go on to a master's abroad.

name: International Business
overview: Year one lays foundations in marketing, accounting, economics, finance and operations, with communication and teamwork skills alongside. Year two deepens finance, marketing, operations and corporate social responsibility through analytical projects. In year three you choose a specialisation in finance, operations or marketing, and can add a minor or electives and study abroad. Lectures, workshops and group projects dominate, with work gradually becoming more independent. The fourth year is a semester-long internship at an international organisation followed by a graduation project on a real business problem. Graduates work as financial analysts, digital marketers, procurement analysts or logistics coordinators.

name: International Communication Management
overview: You begin with global communication contexts, intercultural awareness, organisational communication, research methods, design thinking and marketing basics. Year two turns to public relations, public affairs and communication for the Sustainable Development Goals, and you choose a thematic minor or an exchange abroad. Teaching is mostly project work for real clients such as multinationals, NGOs and The Hague Municipality. Year three covers strategic communication and change management, and ends with a graduation internship of about 15 weeks. Graduates work as communication consultants, PR officers, marketing coordinators or social media managers, and about half continue to a master's.

name: International Financial Management & Control
overview: Year one covers financial accounting, finance and investments, marketing and Excel; year two adds cost accounting, corporate finance, risk management and sustainability. Year three opens with an internship of about six months in the Netherlands or abroad, followed by strategic and risk management. In year four you choose two minors, such as blockchain, data science or FinTech, or study at a partner university, then finish with a second internship and a graduation project. Case studies, study visits and guest speakers support the teaching. Pre-master options lead to master's programmes in accounting, auditing and finance, and graduates work as controllers, analysts and auditors.

name: International Public Policy and Leadership
overview: The programme is organised around five professional areas: advising, advocacy, evaluation, organisation and management, and project-based working, drawing on politics, law, economics and international relations. In year two you plan, run and evaluate your own conference on a global issue. Year three offers three tracks: European governance with a Brussels trip, peace, justice and human rights, or global governance and development. Teaching mixes seminars, study visits and group projects that produce policy briefs and speeches. Year four brings a 20-week internship and a professional product or thesis. Graduates work in NGOs, ministries and international organisations, or take a pre-master toward public administration at Leiden.

name: Process & Food Technology
overview: Year one combines chemistry, mathematics, biotechnology and basic process technology, applied at once in labs and projects such as water treatment and cheese making. In year two you design sustainable production processes with industry partners, using simulation software. Year three offers a minor, for example Food Product Design, and an internship at a company, engineering firm or research institute. In the final year you specialise in food industry processes or chemical process technology and write a thesis at a partner company. Field trips to plants and breweries support the lectures. Graduates work as process or food technologists, product developers and quality or safety engineers, or move on to a master's.

name: Safety and Security Management Studies
overview: Year one covers international law, criminology, psychology, economics and policy making. Year two focuses on industrial safety and international security, with crisis management, geopolitics and conflict studies. In year three you choose three minors from options such as intelligence collection and analysis, health, safety and environmental management, human security, and counterterrorism. Guest lecturers from the intelligence community and military, and visits to military bases and prisons, support the teaching. Year four is an international internship, for example at NATO or OPCW, then a thesis. Graduates work as security risk analysts, policy advisors and security managers, or continue to crisis and security management at Leiden.

name: Sport Studies | International Sport Management
overview: Year one introduces sport and society, international sport management, leadership, ethics, research methods, event management and sport development. Year two moves to strategic management, sport policy, marketing, finance, sponsorship and people management. Learning is practical: students co-organise real events with sponsors, take study trips to European sport organisations and work on applied cases. In year three you shape your own route with a minor, an internship or an exchange abroad, and the final stage is a graduation challenge for a real sports organisation and a thesis. Graduates work as sport development officers, marketers, sponsorship managers and event coordinators.

name: User Experience Design
overview: The first year covers UX and interaction design, research methods, the psychology of experience and programming, with web technologies, mobile platforms, Arduino and sensors. You learn by working on projects for real clients such as Philips, IKEA and Google, in workshops equipped for prototyping, and a field trip to the Ars Electronica Festival in Linz is included. Later years add an internship at a design agency or tech company, a minor such as game development or photography, and an optional exchange. The degree ends with an independent graduation project. Graduates work as UX designers and researchers, interaction and service designers, and front-end or mobile developers.

name: Cognitive Science and Artificial Intelligence
overview: You study how intelligent systems work and how that relates to the human brain, starting with introductory AI, human cognition and programming. Year two adds machine learning, deep learning, human-computer and human-robot interaction, cognitive neuroscience and research experience, with practicals in the Brain and Behavior Lab. Ethics is built into the courses, and teaching is hands-on. In year three you take specialisation courses such as Hybrid Intelligence, use a mobility window for a minor, an internship or other courses, and write a bachelor's thesis. After a master's, graduates work as intelligent software developers, technology consultants, AI researchers or machine learning engineers.

name: Digital Culture and Society
overview: You study digital culture, identity, community and the role of art in society, while building academic writing and research skills. Writing is central: students publish papers and opinion pieces on an online platform with a global readership, alongside search engine optimisation skills. Courses include Exploring Digital Cultures, Digital Media and Politics, and Art and Media in a Digital Society. In year two you choose electives or an internship, and in year three you build a profile with a minor, electives or an exchange and write a thesis. After a master's, graduates work in digital agencies, online journalism, cultural heritage, government and research, as editors, content coordinators or policy officers.

name: Double Bachelor: International Business Administration and Economics
overview: Two bachelor's degrees are combined in one integrated programme, with economics and international business taught side by side from the first semester to the thesis. Year one covers micro- and macroeconomics, marketing, human resources, statistics and programming; later years add finance, strategy, international trade, economic growth, corporate governance, supply chain management, ethics and the effects of technology and data on business. In year four you choose electives, a semester abroad or an internship, and write a thesis in the discipline of your choice. Typical courses include International Finance, Welfare Economics and Comparative and Cross-Cultural Management.

name: Economics
overview: You learn how people, firms and governments decide and how those decisions shape whole economies, using economic models and data. Year one builds the micro- and macroeconomic foundation with mathematics and statistics as tools; year two goes deeper into both and adds courses such as Development Economics and International Trade. In year three you can study a semester abroad, do an internship, or stay for minors in economics and business and electives, then write a thesis. Typical courses include Welfare Economics and International Finance. Graduates work as economists or data analysts in international organisations, banks, multinationals and research centres.

name: Econometrics and Operations Research
overview: The first year pairs mathematics and statistics courses with economics and business courses, and runs alongside the Improving Society Lab, where you apply econometrics to real problems such as optimising medical treatment or distributing humanitarian aid. From year two you add asset pricing, stochastic operations research models and communication skills. In year three you specialise in one of the three main fields of econometrics, and can spend six months on exchange abroad, and the programme closes with a bachelor's thesis. After a master's, graduates work as supply chain specialists, quantitative analysts or business intelligence specialists.

name: Entrepreneurship and Business Innovation
overview: Courses in entrepreneurship, business innovation, business fundamentals and statistics run alongside the Entrepreneurship in Action series, in which you apply entrepreneurial methods in real projects. Year one has two such projects, one on exploring opportunities and one on building solutions. Year two covers law, finance, leadership and ethics, creative problem-solving, and entrepreneurship in start-ups, established companies and social ventures. In year three you can study abroad, do an internship or take a minor, then choose a specialisation course and finish with a graduation project. Many graduates start their own company or join a start-up, or go on to a master's.

name: Global Law
overview: The programme covers the traditional legal subjects, such as contract, tort, criminal, administrative, property and constitutional law, but compares different legal systems rather than one. Year one introduces law, justice and legal history, with interdisciplinary work alongside economists and sociologists. From year two the focus moves to legal courses, including EU law and public international law. In year three you can go on exchange or stay for minors, and you write a thesis; typical courses include Business for Lawyers and Law, Technology and Society. After a master's, graduates work as consultants, legal advisers or compliance analysts, with alumni at NATO, the European Parliament and the International Criminal Court.

name: Global Management of Social Issues
overview: You tackle complex 'wicked problems' such as poverty, migration, climate change and humanitarian emergencies from an organisational and management angle, combining organisation and management studies, human resource studies and sociology. Year one adds social psychology, and year two brings philosophy and international law plus a simulation in which you join a humanitarian emergency response team. Courses include Wicked Problems 101, International Organizations and Advanced Project Management. In year three you do a project internship with an internationally active organisation, an exchange abroad or minors, and write a bachelor's thesis.

name: Human Resource Studies: People Management
overview: The programme has an international slant with an emphasis on Europe, and links to large international companies. Year one introduces psychology, sociology, economics and management studies and starts applying them to work, organisations and people management. Year two combines these perspectives on strategic, financial and managerial aspects of HR, employee development, health and wellbeing, and teaches you to advise organisations on people policy. In year three you explore people management in an international setting and use a mobility window to study abroad, do an internship or take a minor, before writing a bachelor's thesis. Typical courses include Strategic HRM, Talent Management and Cross Cultural HRM.

name: International Business Administration
overview: The programme looks at how a large global organisation is run and how it relates to the world around it. Year one covers finance and investment, international strategy, human resource management, marketing, mathematics, statistics and programming, plus how AI and data change business. Year two adds management accounting, global sustainable leadership, cross-cultural management and ethics. In year three you specialise through a minor, a semester abroad or an internship, and write a thesis in a business discipline. After a master's, graduates work as consultants, supply chain managers or business analysts, with alumni at firms such as PwC, ASML and ABN AMRO.

name: International Sociology
overview: You study society from a comparative perspective on the Western world, and carry out a sociological research project every year. Year one introduces sociology alongside political science, social psychology and research methods. In year two you choose a specialisation, either Culture in Comparative Perspective or Social Risks in a Changing World, and finish the year with a research project in that field. Year three leaves room for minors, electives, study abroad or an internship, and you write a thesis in your specialisation. After a master's, graduates work as sociology teachers or journalists, and alumni have joined ministries, research agencies, newspapers and companies such as ING and Philips.

name: Psychology
overview: You build a foundation across all areas of psychology in year one, along with academic skills and research methods. In year two you pick one of nine majors, among them clinical, forensic, developmental, economic, social, and work and organisational psychology, and take statistics, specialisation courses and supervised small-group research. Year three finishes the major with a professional practice course, a minor, two electives and a bachelor's thesis, and you can study abroad for six months. Teaching combines lectures with lab research, tutorials and group assignments. Typical courses include Brain and Behavior and Personality Psychology.

name: Theology
overview: The programme spans fields from biblical studies to spirituality, using history, philosophy, literature and the social sciences to reflect on questions of meaning, identity, tradition and values. Year one maps the main fields of theology and introduces Greek and Hebrew; year two goes deeper and adds Latin. Courses include Comparative Religion, on Islam, Buddhism and Hinduism, Systematic Philosophy, and reading the Bible in its original languages. Year three opens a semester mobility window for electives, other programmes or courses abroad, and ends with a bachelor's thesis on a topic of your choice.

name: University College Tilburg: Liberal Arts and Sciences
overview: A broad first year of core courses and academic skills leads to a choice of major: Law, Politics and Culture; Cognitive Neuroscience and Behavior; Interdisciplinary Social Sciences; or Design and Technology. From year two you link your major to a theme shared across majors: Transformations to Sustainability, Democracy and Justice, or Technology and Society, and apply knowledge to real-world problems. In year three you take a minor or exchange abroad and complete two final projects: a bachelor's thesis and a Societal Capstone applying your knowledge to real-life projects. Courses include Evil, Public Law and Democracy, and Brain and Behavior, in small classes.

name: Applied Mathematics
overview: You learn to build a mathematical model of a practical problem, solve it, and translate the answer back so specialists in other fields can use it, with examples from mobile technology, cybersecurity, logistics, medical imaging and car design. Teaching follows challenge-based learning: lectures and small-group practical sessions, with problems tackled in groups and project work growing over the three years. Besides compulsory mathematics courses you take non-technology courses and a large share of free electives, and a double bachelor with Applied Physics or Computer Science and Engineering is possible. Graduates become cryptologists, logistics consultants, statisticians and software designers, or continue to a two-year master's.

name: Applied Physics
overview: You study the physics of light and sound, flow and heat, atoms and particles, and build skills in experimental design, data handling, automation and computational physics. About three quarters of the programme is core physics and mathematics, and a quarter is electives that deepen physics or reach into other TU/e fields, with courses on the impact of technology. Teams tackle technological and societal challenges, and you can join student teams such as Solid or Polar. The programme ends with a Bachelor End Project, either in a research group or on an open problem from companies or student teams. Graduates enter a master's such as Applied Physics, Nuclear Fusion or quantum science, or work in chip manufacturing and research institutes.

name: Architecture, Urbanism and Building Sciences
overview: The programme joins architecture, urbanism, building sciences, structural design and real estate, looking at how the living environment is built and keeps changing. You can follow one of three profiles from the start, building physics and structural design, architectural urban design and engineering, or urban systems and real estate, and choose electives to shape your own route. Teaching mixes lectures, guided self-study and challenge-based design projects done in multidisciplinary teams, starting with a first-year studio. Year two builds the structural engineering core, and year three is dominated by a final project. Graduates continue to a master's and work in architecture firms, construction, housing associations and government.

name: Automotive Technology
overview: You study the car as a system, combining mechanical engineering with electronics and software for electric, automated and connected vehicles. Half of the curriculum is automotive courses and half is core subjects such as mathematics, natural sciences and multidisciplinary design, with a quarter given to electives. A learning pathway on users, society and enterprise looks at the impact of technology on people. Teaching is lectures, guided self-study and challenge-based projects on real cases, ending with an individual Bachelor End Project. The degree is awarded as electrical engineering with an automotive specialisation, and the Brainport Eindhoven region, home to much of the Dutch automotive industry, provides employers.

name: Chemical Engineering and Chemistry
overview: You combine chemistry, materials science and process engineering, from how molecules are built to scaling a process up to continuous production. Year one stresses mathematics and physics with inorganic, physical and bio-chemistry, and lab sessions right after lectures. Year two adds kinetics, polymer chemistry, separation technology and challenge-based projects on societal issues, and year three is an independent final project in a research group. From year two you pick electives, including themes such as AI, energy and sustainability, and take ethics-of-technology courses. Most students go on to a master's, and the degree is internationally accredited by the IChemE.

name: Computer Science and Engineering
overview: After a base of calculus, statistics, linear algebra and logic, you follow three learning lines throughout: systems (security, networks, databases), software development, and algorithms and theory of computing. In year one you build a user-friendly web portal; in year two you work with students from other programmes on an open problem tied to the Sustainable Development Goals; in year three you take an in-depth course and join a ten-week group project on open-source software before the Bachelor Final Project. Two courses cover engineering ethics and engineering for society. Graduates become software or app developers, or take a master's in Computer Science and Engineering or Embedded Systems.

name: Data Science
overview: This is a joint programme of Eindhoven and Tilburg, so you attend classes at both universities. It is organised in six learning lines: law and ethics, computer science, business, data analytics, data challenges and cognitive science, with courses in statistics, programming, data mining and business analytics. In the data challenges line, teams solve real problems using large data sets from different fields. Electives let you aim for a master's, for example through packages in advanced data science or finance and risk, or minors in business and entrepreneurship or cognitive science and AI. The programme ends with a Bachelor End Project and leads to master's degrees in data science, business analytics or marketing analytics.

name: Electrical Engineering
overview: You learn the fundamentals of electricity and magnetism through three societal themes: communication, such as chips using light signals and wireless protocols, healthcare, such as MRI scanners and electromagnetic therapies, and sustainable energy systems. Half of the curriculum is electrical engineering major subjects, the rest core subjects and a quarter electives, plus a pathway on the impact of technology on society. Teaching combines lectures, guided self-study and challenge-based projects, supported by part-time professors, guest lectures and excursions with companies in the Brainport Eindhoven region. Each student completes an individual Bachelor End Project.

name: Industrial Design
overview: You learn to turn technology into products and services, balancing data, creativity, user needs, aesthetics, social impact and business across five areas: business and entrepreneurship, creativity and aesthetics, math, data and computing, technology and realization, and user and society. Learning is self-directed and hands-on, with prototypes made to test ideas and multidisciplinary squads working on social themes and presenting at a Demo Day each semester. From year two you deepen your strongest area, using electives in design or other departments. Year three brings an exchange, internship or minor elsewhere, then a Final Bachelor Project. Graduates become product, UX and service designers, innovation consultants or entrepreneurs.

name: Industrial Engineering
overview: You treat business processes as systems that can be analysed, modelled and improved, using mathematics, data science and AI models. The core covers occupational and organisational psychology, operational management, product innovation and information systems, alongside statistics, data engineering and an ethics course on the impact of technology. Teaching includes field trips, company partnerships, a multidisciplinary challenge-based project in year two and many electives, half of year three, to broaden or deepen your studies. The degree ends with a final project at an external organisation, where you answer a research question about a business case.

name: Mechanical Engineering
overview: You combine mathematics, physics and chemistry with heat and flow, mechanics, dynamics, control theory and material properties, to design and improve mechanical products and production processes. Year one includes CAD and NX training for 3D design, year two adds thermodynamics and the control of mechanical systems, and about 30 percent of the curriculum is challenge-based projects tackled in groups. Year three offers electives and a Bachelor Final Project in a faculty research group, with past topics including humanoid robots and chip factory modelling. Graduates work in machine manufacturing, research institutes, start-ups and multinationals.

name: Psychology & Technology
overview: You study how technology shapes people and how to design technology around human needs, for example household robots, smart lighting and intelligent infrastructure. Year one is a fixed mix of about half psychology and half technology, with around two days a week on group design and research assignments. In the first quarter you choose a specialisation such as Robotics, ICT or Living, and from year two a quarter of the programme is free electives. Challenge-based projects bring in students from other departments, and year three ends with an individual Bachelor End Project including a scientific report.

name: Sustainable Innovation
overview: The programme joins technology with sustainability, economics, policy and social science, to train people who can assess innovations and drive change. Three learning lines run through it: transitions, with courses such as Navigating Sustainability Transitions; assessment, using life-cycle assessment and cost-benefit analysis; and economic policy, including Economics of Innovation. You work on cases with companies, governments and societal organisations through challenge-based learning, and choose electives within the programme or from other TU/e programmes. Year three brings the perspectives together to assess innovations and support decisions, and the location in Brainport Eindhoven provides innovation partners.

name: Liberal Arts & Sciences
overview: There is no fixed major: you design your own curriculum from courses across fields such as politics, psychology, data science, environmental studies and media, and the offer changes each year with student interests and current events. Classes are small and international, and the emphasis is on thinking across disciplines and reasoning independently. Professional and Personal Development is compulsory in the first year, and Community-Engaged Learning links coursework to local organisations. Students live in a close-knit residential community in Middelburg. Graduates go into sustainability, law, business, public health, politics and data science, or on to graduate study.

name: Liberal Arts and Sciences (University College Utrecht)
overview: You assemble your own curriculum from more than 20 disciplines across humanities, social sciences and sciences, taking at least one course in each domain in year one. You declare a major in year two, with room for electives, a minor, study abroad or an internship. Classes average about 20 students and rely on discussion, presentations and group work, with continuous assessment rather than single final exams. A personal tutor guides your choices. Year three is advanced coursework and an individual research thesis in your major, and the degree is awarded as a Bachelor of Arts or Science, leading to master's programmes or work.

name: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences
overview: The programme follows drug development from the first question to the finished product. Year one has four compulsory courses on the drug pipeline: clinical development, how drugs and the body interact, the drug and the cell, and the drug molecule. Year two adds immunopharmacology, psychopharmacology, analytical methods and pharmaceutical biotechnology, plus electives, and year three is mostly electives such as Medicinal Chemistry or Omics in Oncology. Teaching is project-based, with frequent labs run by active researchers and classes of at most 60. You carry out your own research project in year three in a research group at Utrecht University or its medical centre.

name: Economics and Business Economics
overview: You study macroeconomics, microeconomics, international economics and business economics, with first-year courses such as Mathematics for Economists, Accounting and Finance, Statistics and Strategy and Organisation. Year two adds econometrics and corporate finance, and year three centres on electives and an applied economics research course. Nearly half of the programme is optional: a dedicated minor can link economics to law, geography, social sciences or applied data science, and the bachelor thesis can sit between economics and that minor. You can also do an internship abroad or study at a partner university, including a year in Rome.

name: English Language and Culture
overview: You study how English has changed and varies across groups of speakers, read literature from the English-speaking world, and train your pronunciation within a World Englishes approach. Year one includes The Sound Lab, The Writers' Lab, and literature and language history courses from the Renaissance onward. In year two you choose one of five specialisations, among them language learning and teaching, transforming texts, the social life of English and Celtic literatures and linguistics, alongside an integrated humanities track. One third of the programme is electives, and internships in the Netherlands or abroad, for example with publishers, translation agencies and schools, are possible. Year three ends with a thesis.

name: Global Sustainability Science
overview: You combine mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology with management, economics and innovation to understand sustainability from local to global scale. Year one ends with fieldwork on Texel island, and in year two you pick one of five tracks, from water, climate and ecosystems to business and innovation, and work on a Global Transformation Project. In year three, track courses lead to a Consultancy Project advising real clients such as NGOs, governments and businesses, then a thesis. A quarter of the courses are electives, and you can study abroad for up to six months. Teaching draws on researchers at the Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development.

name: History
overview: Year one surveys European history from antiquity to the present within a global frame, with research labs on source analysis and a course introducing quantitative methods. In year two you choose one of seven specialisations in two tracks: History, with themes such as political conflict in modern Europe or crises and inequality, or International Relations in Historical Perspective, including Europe in the World and conflict and security. Each ends in research seminars where you work on a historiographical debate. Year three offers electives, an internship, a minor or a semester abroad, and a thesis on a topic of your choice. Tutorials of about 20 to 25 students and excursions are central.

name: Linguistics
overview: Year one introduces the study of language through courses on meaning, psychology of language, morphosyntax, sociolinguistics, phonetics, language development and digital tools. In year two you choose one of three clusters: Language and Society (taught in Dutch), Language and Cognition, covering psycholinguistics and acquisition, or Language and Computation, covering corpora, computational modelling and language models, alongside an integrated humanities track. Year three has a capstone course on research and writing, electives for one third of the programme, and a bachelor's thesis. You can do an internship, with past placements at dictionary and language institutes.

name: Literary Studies
overview: Year one covers literary history from antiquity to the present, close reading, cultural criticism and current theoretical debates such as affect theory and environmental criticism. In year two you choose a specialisation, Literature across Borders, with postcolonial, migration and ecological themes, or Literature in Conflict, covering banned books, contested memory and dissent, and join an integrated humanities track. Year three includes The Republic of Letters, on publishing, festivals and cultural careers, electives for one third of the programme, and a thesis. You can intern at publishing houses and cultural institutions in the Netherlands or abroad.

name: Media and Culture
overview: Year one introduces the media landscape, storytelling, new media and digital culture, film, television, and theatre and dance, with research methods. In year two you choose one of four profiles: participatory cultures and sustainable futures, critical AI and global digital culture, media heritage and curation, or performing arts and creative technologies, together with an integrated humanities track. Year three has a research seminar, a thesis and electives for one third of the programme. Tutorial groups are small, and internships are possible at institutions such as EYE Film Museum in Amsterdam and the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision.

name: Molecular and Biophysical Life Sciences
overview: Year one lays a foundation in biology, chemistry and physics with courses such as Cell Biology, Mathematics and Programming, Physical Chemistry, Biomolecular Chemistry and Biological Physics. In years two and three you take twelve electives, at least six within the major and up to six from the whole university catalogue, organised in four themes: Genes to Organisms, Molecules and Cells, Molecules and Medicine, and Biophysics and Modelling. The programme finishes with a bachelor thesis, a research project of your own under the supervision of scientific staff.

name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics
overview: Year one has eight compulsory courses across philosophy, politics, economics and history, including Political Philosophy, Microeconomics, Macroeconomics and Comparative Democratic Institutions. Year two adds methods in qualitative research, statistics and epistemology, and one of four thematic packages: Challenges to the Welfare State, Markets and Regulators, Global Pathways to a Sustainable Future, or Democracy and its Discontents, each ending in an individual interdisciplinary research paper. Year three leaves free space for courses elsewhere or an internship, and finishes with the PPE thesis. Students have worked at banks, international organisations, embassies and ministries.

name: Actuarial Science
overview: Year one builds foundations in calculus, linear algebra, probability theory, microeconomics, macroeconomics, finance and programming in R and Python. Year two moves to life insurance mathematics, risk theory, machine learning for quantitative economics, econometrics and a research seminar. In the first semester of year three you can do an internship, study abroad or take a minor or electives, and the second brings specialised courses such as stochastic models in life insurance and the bachelor's thesis. A Dutch-start track and an English track cover the same content. Graduates are sought after in insurance and many other sectors, and can continue to a master's and then certification as an actuary.

name: Ancient Studies
overview: You study the history, literature, art, philosophy and material culture of the ancient world, from a wide geographical and time perspective. Year one includes Objects in Context, The Classical Canon and a cultural history of the ancient world; later courses cover Mediterranean cultural contact and religion in antiquity, with an excursion abroad in year two. You choose a specialisation in ancient history, archaeology, Ancient Near Eastern Studies including Akkadian, or Latin or Greek for Dutch speakers. The degree is shared with another Amsterdam university, so lecturers and classes come from both, and there is free space for a minor, internship or study abroad. A bachelor's thesis shows interdisciplinary analysis.

name: Archaeology
overview: You study past societies and what they mean today, working with materials such as pottery, coins and bones, reconstructing landscapes, and learning digital recording and forensic methods. Year one includes What is Archaeology? and a first field school in excavation, and year two adds Science in Archaeology, Archaeology and the City and a second field school. Excavation projects run on Terschelling in the Netherlands and in Greece. Year three covers publishing excavation results and ends with a bachelor thesis, and there is free space for a minor, internship or study abroad. It is a joint degree with another Amsterdam university, with ties to the city archaeological service and the Allard Pierson Museum.

name: Business Administration
overview: You study how businesses are managed, covering strategy, marketing, finance, organisation, international business and digital business, with attention to social responsibility and AI. Year one is built on organisation, people, economics and methods, and year two adds marketing, finance and information management and a plan for starting your own business. In the first semester of year three you assemble your own route from an internship, study abroad, a minor or electives; the second brings a specialisation in accounting and control, entrepreneurship, finance, or the future of management and AI, and a thesis. Cases from real, international companies drive the teaching, in a Dutch-start or English track.

name: Business Analytics
overview: Mathematics, programming, AI and machine learning, and the use of big data in business sit at the centre. Year one covers calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, learning programming from scratch, and opens with a course on real-life data cases. Year two adds machine learning, operations research, econometrics, and options such as HR analytics and an entrepreneurship hackathon. In year three you can do an internship, study abroad, a minor or electives, then take text retrieval and mining, marketing analytics and a thesis based on a data challenge. Ethics runs through the courses, including AI, privacy and cybersecurity, and graduates have direct access to the university's master's in Data Science and Business Analytics.

name: Computational Social Science
overview: You combine the social sciences with data skills, programming in Python, user experience design, web development, machine learning and responsible AI, to work on challenges such as climate change, health and inequality. Learning is project-based, with real clients setting weekly projects instead of exams. Each year has two semester-long courses: climate and digital surveillance in year one, health, mobility and inequality in year two, including network analysis and language processing. Year three is a capstone project with external partners, electives or a minor, and an internship or exchange semester. Weekly check-ins with tutors guide you.

name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
overview: You learn to study people through in-depth qualitative research and face-to-face fieldwork. Year one covers introductory anthropology, ethnographies and academic writing, research methods and current debates, and a mentor supports you throughout. In year two you take exploration courses such as Body and Culture or Power and Politics and a regional course, for example on Latin America or urban Africa, and practise ethnography with your own fieldwork and report. Year three has a thematic course in an area such as visual anthropology, plus career-focused courses. You have free electives for a minor, an internship or an exchange, and the programme is taught in English or a bilingual track.

name: Econometrics and Data Science
overview: Year one covers calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, economics, finance and Python, with introductions to econometrics in R and to data science. Year two adds advanced mathematics, machine learning for quantitative economics, econometrics, mathematical economics and a group empirical project. In year three the first semester is free for an internship, study abroad, a minor or electives, and the second combines a thesis with a specialisation: econometrics, on causal models and policy analysis, or data science, with language technologies and reinforcement learning. You learn to advise organisations on the impact of their strategies and to support decisions with data analysis. A Dutch-language track has the same content.

name: Economics and Business Economics
overview: Year one covers mathematics, principles of economics and business, accounting, microeconomics, macroeconomics, statistics and finance, and ends with a research project. In year two you study money and banking, econometrics, international finance and methodology, then choose a major: Economics, with game theory and advanced micro and macro, or Business Economics, with corporate law, strategy, accounting and finance. A research laboratory brings you into real projects. Year three starts with a semester of your choice, an internship, study abroad, a minor or electives, followed by a specialisation in accounting and control, finance or organisational economics for business economists, and a thesis.

name: English Language and Culture
overview: The first year combines literature courses, from genres and theory to early modern and eighteenth-century texts, with linguistics, including the history of English, global varieties, phonology and grammar, and a course in rhetoric and writing. In years two and three you follow one of two tracks, World Literatures in English or English Linguistics and Literature, with restricted-choice courses and electives. Year three has three capstone seminars and a thesis. There is free space for a minor, internship or study abroad, and a scheme lets you spend the third year at a British or Irish university. The degree builds argument, presentation and research skills.

name: European Studies
overview: Year one introduces Europe through its history, culture and politics, European integration and democracy, and European identities and cultures, alongside four language courses in a modern language chosen from about twenty, including Danish, German, Polish and Turkish. From year two you choose one of six majors: European Culture, History, East European Studies, Law, Politics or Economics, and take Philosophy of the Humanities. Space is left for programme-related electives, a minor or free electives, an internship and study abroad through Erasmus or global exchange, and the degree ends with a bachelor's thesis. Weekly workload averages around 42 hours.

name: Global Arts, Culture and Politics
overview: Year one covers art and media, sustainability, cultural policy and AI, with courses such as Culture Wars, Historicising the Global and Fake News: Introducing the Human and AI. In year two you choose one of four majors: Curating the Past, Reimagining Sustainability, Culture and Social Justice, or The Human and Artificial Intelligence, and begin a thesis research lab. Skills courses teach academic writing, visual and digital literacy, archival research and interviewing. Year three brings electives, a minor and a thesis or final project, with internships possible in journalism, curating, theatre and research. Graduates work in museums, heritage institutions, archives and the wider cultural sector.

name: Global Communication Science (Communication Science)
overview: Year one covers global and comparative perspectives on communication, research basics, media innovations, crises and resilience, and a skills bootcamp. Year two deepens research methods, with statistics and qualitative approaches, and thematic courses on marketing and entertainment and on health and sustainability. A compulsory internship at an international organisation ends with an advisory report, which sets this programme apart. In year three there is room for electives, a minor such as Communication in the Digital Society, or an exchange semester, and complete an independent communication research project. Networking events and guest lectures prepare you for work in international organisations and communication.

name: Human Geography and Planning
overview: Year one introduces human geography and spatial planning, GIS, urban dynamics with Amsterdam as a case, and research methods, ending with a group project on the Amsterdam region. In year two you carry out a research project in the Netherlands and one abroad with one to two weeks of fieldwork, and choose thematic electives such as migration, development or environmental change. Three specialisations are available: Planning, Human Geography and Global Urbanism. Year three has a thesis based on your own data collection, with free space for a minor, research internship or a semester at one of the partner universities. Fieldwork with external clients builds practical skills.

name: Linguistics
overview: Year one introduces linguistics, phonetics, morphology and sociolinguistics, with a language of your choice, such as Arabic, Czech, French, German, Spanish, Turkish or Sign Language of the Netherlands, and a research project on language acquisition. Year two covers phonology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics, analysis of an unfamiliar language, and courses on first language acquisition, psycholinguistics and neurolinguistics. In year three you tailor your studies through specialisation options, electives or a minor, with space for an internship or study abroad, and write a bachelor's thesis. Graduates go into academia, teaching, research and many fields where the analytical skills transfer.

name: Literary and Cultural Analysis (Literary Studies)
overview: You learn to read literature, art and popular culture closely and to reflect on what they mean today. Year one covers poetic and visual analysis, discourse analysis and narratology, world literature, contemporary arts and media, and cultural memory. Year two adds literary and cultural theory, art, science and technology, and a case-study course, and in a Public Interventions assignment you design an unexpected situation in public space to study culture. Year three has a thesis workshop, current debates and a thesis, with electives such as Decolonial Thought or Moving Images Across Media. You have space for a minor, an internship or study abroad.

name: Media and Culture
overview: Year one covers media aesthetics, media theory, media research and the transformation of media culture, with courses called Doing Media Studies that build practical and creative skills. In years two and three you follow one of two tracks: Film Studies, on film history, theory and global cinema alongside filmmaking, or Television and Cross-Media Culture, on serial forms and digital platforms. Both include practice-based production in small groups, making a short film, documentary or television programme. Year three has space for electives, a minor, an internship or study abroad, and a thesis on a topic of your choice.

name: Media and Information
overview: Year one covers media in everyday life, digital culture, algorithms and platforms, media theory and research, and practical problem-solving courses. In years two and three you choose a major: Cultural Information Studies, using data analysis, programming basics and computational humanities methods on archives, Wikipedia and social media, or New Media and Digital Culture, studying how digital media and AI shape society. You have space for electives, a minor or an internship in a media organisation, and study abroad is possible. The skills fit creative industries, journalism and administration.

name: Political Science
overview: The first phase covers a broad introduction: history of Europe, political thought, public policy and governance, international relations and law and politics, with attention to conflict, cooperation and power. In year two you choose one of five tracks: International Relations, Comparative Politics, Public Policy and Governance, Political Theory or Political Economy, and do a research project. Year three offers electives and a work placement, study abroad, minor or language study, and ends with an independent thesis. Placements have included the UN, EU embassies, think tanks and NGOs, and graduates go into policymaking, journalism and international organisations.

name: Psychology
overview: Year one covers all the subdisciplines, including neuropsychology, social, developmental, work and organisational and clinical psychology, cognitive neuroscience, research methods and statistics with practical training groups. In year two you learn to turn a psychological question into a study, then choose one of the majors: Work and Organisational Psychology, Psychological Methods, Brain and Cognition, Social Psychology, Clinical Psychology or Clinical Developmental Psychology. Year three starts with a bachelor's thesis and then lets you take a second major, a minor such as communication science or law, or an exchange. English and Dutch tracks share the content.

name: Sign Language Linguistics (Linguistics)
overview: You study how sign languages are structured while learning Sign Language of the Netherlands yourself, over four levels in year one. First-year courses include introductions to linguistics and sign linguistics, transcription of sign languages, morphology and sociolinguistics. Years two and three cover the phonology, morphology, syntax, lexicon and psycholinguistics of sign languages, semantics and pragmatics, linguistic theories and research methods, ending in a bachelor's thesis. You have space for a minor, electives or study abroad, and internships are possible at the Dutch Sign Center, in hospital clinical linguistics or in research.

name: Sociology
overview: Year one teaches sociological theory, research methodology, statistics, philosophy of social science and the sociology of institutions, with an Amsterdam Research Project in qualitative methods. Year two lets you explore six domains: urban society, race, gender and sexuality, migration and citizenship, globalising cultures, health and society, and education and work, with advanced statistics, theory and qualitative analysis. In year three you have elective space for specialising or a minor, an exchange or internship, and a Bachelor Research Project, an independent study within a group project that produces a thesis. English and bilingual tracks are offered.

name: Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics (PPLE)
overview: Politics, psychology, law and economics are combined so that you approach social challenges through all four lenses, in small tutorial groups. Year one has core courses in each discipline, such as Politics, Power and Governance, Law, Justice and Morality and Psychology and Society, plus integrative seminars on human rights and solidarity, and you pick a major by the end of the year. In years two and three about half your courses are in your major, politics, psychology, law, or economics and business, and half stay interdisciplinary, ending in a bachelor's thesis. You can add an exchange semester. Graduates go into policy, consultancy and research, or master's in law, economics, policy or psychology.

name: Artificial Intelligence
overview: The focus is hybrid intelligence: AI that works with people, and is designed to be effective, trustworthy and socially responsible. Year one builds computational thinking and how AI interacts with people; year two applies this to real cases, such as programming a robot for a real environment or using AI for challenges in healthcare and law. Electives let you lean toward the social side of AI or toward technical depth in algorithms, data and computer science. In year three you take a minor, which can be abroad, and write a bachelor's thesis. Graduates work as software developers, data scientists, machine learning engineers or analysts, or continue to a master's in AI.

name: Business Analytics
overview: The programme is about half data analysis and mathematics, a third computer science and the rest business, and is taught by both the mathematics and computer science departments. Year one covers calculus, Python programming, linear algebra, probability, operations research and accounting, with practical projects. Year two adds statistics, stochastic modelling, R, C++ and SQL, business intelligence, finance and a big data project. In year three you take a minor, machine learning and combinatorial optimisation, and a group Bachelor Project: Business Case with an external company. Cases have involved IBM, Deloitte and Dutch Railways, and exchange places are available.

name: Communication Science
overview: You study how people use media and communicate, drawing on psychology, sociology, media studies and marketing. Year one covers media use and organisational communication, with courses in journalism and interpersonal communication; year two turns to marketing and political communication, including the psychology of persuasion, health campaigns and social media analytics. Four project-based courses link study to professionals, and research methods and statistics run alongside. In year three you choose an internship, study abroad or a minor, and write a bachelor's thesis. Graduates work as communication advisers, PR officers, campaign designers, media analysts and journalists.

name: Computer Science
overview: Year one gives a broad base: programming, logic, data structures and algorithms, web technology, computer organisation, networks, requirements engineering and a Systems Programming Project in which you design and build a computing system. Year two covers operating systems, databases, software design and functional programming, plus three electives such as AI or software engineering. In year three you take a semester-long minor, for example Bioinformatics or Business Analytics and Data Science, then automata, machine learning, ethics and a Bachelor's Project supervised by researchers. Graduates work as software developers, data scientists and IT consultants, or continue to a master's.

name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
overview: You study how culture, power and identity shape each other in issues such as climate, migration and inequality. Year one covers anthropological theory, ethnographic and social research methods, the global history of inequality and statistics, with masterclasses on three professional tracks: researcher, practitioner and creative professional. In year two you choose a profile and study development, political and economic anthropology, nation and migration, and urban studies. Year three centres on ethnographic fieldwork for a Bachelor Project in the Netherlands or abroad, including Colombia, ending in an academic article, a policy report or a documentary, photo or podcast project.

name: Econometrics and Data Science
overview: You learn to solve problems in economics and business with econometric models, machine learning, time series and statistics, for example predicting inflation or forecasting inventory. Year one covers calculus, linear algebra, programming, statistics, finance and macroeconomics, with an introduction to data science. Year two adds data structures, econometrics, databases and a small-group Data Science Project on real cases. In year three you take a minor or study abroad, take machine learning and robust statistics, and write a thesis on a topic you choose. Group work and company contacts run through the degree, and the study association organises company visits.

name: Econometrics and Operations Research
overview: You use quantitative techniques to investigate and solve problems in economics, business and finance, from banking systems to healthcare resources. Year one covers calculus, programming, linear algebra, probability, macroeconomics and finance, with an introduction to the three specialisation areas. Year two goes deeper into econometrics, operations research and mathematical economics, with numerical methods, case studies and group projects. In year three you take a minor or study abroad, choose a specialisation in econometrics, operations research or mathematical economics, and write a thesis on a subject of your interest. Minors range from closely related fields to political science.

name: Economics and Business Economics
overview: Year one covers microeconomics, macroeconomics, accounting, finance, marketing, programming for economists and quantitative research methods, and ends with an essay and the choice between General Economics and Business Economics. In year two, business economists specialise in accounting, finance or marketing, with courses in research methods, ethics, law and a research paper, in smaller groups. In year three you design the first semester yourself: a minor, for instance in psychology or sociology, study abroad or an internship. The second semester is for the thesis and your specialisation, and all courses are taught in English.

name: History and International Studies
overview: You study Western and non-Western history from antiquity onward together with international relations. Year one covers academic skills, modern Europe, world history from 1000 to the present, and current debates in global history. In year two you choose a regional focus, such as Southeast Asia, Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East or China, and take courses like Capitalism and Inequality, Oral History and History by Numbers, with research seminars. In the first semester of year three you can do an internship, study abroad or take a minor, then work on independent research for a bachelor thesis.

name: International Business Administration
overview: Year one covers business mathematics, organisation theory, global sustainability, accounting and global supply chain management, with a mentoring programme and academic skills. Year two adds business information systems, economics in a global era, finance, and qualitative and quantitative research methods, plus electives. Year three starts with a compulsory semester abroad at one of more than 150 partner universities, then electives, an ethics course and a bachelor's thesis. The IBA Lab has you work with real organisations on complex business challenges, and research participation courses build research skills.

name: Law in Society
overview: Instead of the usual legal divisions, the programme is built around four themes: security, migration, sustainability and market globalisation, showing how several areas of law meet in one social problem. Year one covers security, with criminology, terrorism and philosophy of law, and then markets, including the platform economy, with statistics and psychology. Year two covers migration law and global migration governance and then sustainability, climate change, AI and law and ethics. Sociology, psychology and criminology run through the degree. Year three has a minor, a bachelor's thesis and recap courses in criminal, public and private law.

name: Literature and Society: English
overview: You explore how literature, language and creativity shape society, reading canonical and contemporary English-language literature from the early modern period onward alongside film, television, comics, graphic novels and digital media. The programme combines literary study with linguistics, creative writing and the practice of the publishing industry, and looks at how technology, including AI, changes the way language and literature are produced. It links historical voices to current social, political and cultural questions. Graduates can aim at editorial and publishing work such as editing, copyediting and marketing.

name: Mathematics
overview: Year one covers linear algebra, calculus, discrete mathematics, group theory, analysis, probability and Python programming, with mathematical modelling and typesetting skills. In year two you choose one of seven paths: Algebra and Geometry, Analysis and Dynamical Systems, Probability and Statistics, Biomedical Mathematics, Computer Science, Data Science, or Optimisation and Economics, with Fourier analysis, numerical methods and a Project Mathematics course. Year three includes a minor, or an education track toward teaching in secondary schools, and a Bachelor Project, which can be built on an internship with an outside organisation.

name: Media, Art, Design and Architecture
overview: A common first year covers visual and material culture, European cultural history, the history of media, art, design and architecture, image and object analysis and research methods. In year two you choose Media, Art, Design or Architecture, with track courses such as film and media history, modern art, graphic design and fashion theory, or urbanism and landscape architecture, plus shared courses on exhibitions and urban culture, and an excursion abroad. Year three has five months of free study, a minor, research internship or semester abroad, followed by a research seminar and a bachelor thesis.

name: Philosophy
overview: Year one introduces logic and argumentation, epistemology, ethics, philosophy in global antiquity and contemporary European thought. Year two covers historical, practical and theoretical philosophy, from analytic philosophy and political philosophy to metaphysics and philosophy of mind, with two text seminars and electives. In year three you take a minor from another faculty and two electives, and write a thesis with training and tutoring support, choosing your own topic, problem and supervisor. English and Dutch tracks are offered, and a second study programme can be combined with philosophy.

name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE)
overview: Year one has core courses in ethics, microeconomics and political science, with mathematics, logic and statistics and PPE in Practice courses linking theory to real problems. In year two you choose two of three tracks, philosophy, politics or economics, such as political philosophy, global governance and international relations, or macroeconomics and policy, with electives like global justice, EU studies or behavioural economics. Year three lets you study abroad or do a five-month internship, and ends with a thesis. Graduates work as policymakers, consultants, reporters or academics in banks, governments, think tanks and universities.

name: Political Science: Global Politics
overview: Year one introduces comparative politics, international relations, the politics of social problems, research methods, statistics and political thought, with visits to political institutions and Model United Nations exercises. Year two covers global governance, global political economy, the EU in the global order, and quantitative and qualitative research projects, plus Social Science for Society electives with sociology and communication science students. In year three the first semester is free for study abroad, an internship such as at an embassy or NGO, or a minor in social sciences, economics or law. The second semester is a Graduation Project Global Politics.

name: Psychology
overview: The programme starts broad and then specialises. Year one covers biological, cognitive, social and developmental psychology, personality, psychopathology, research methods, statistics and communication skills. Year two adds neuropsychology, work and organisational psychology, genes and environment, interviewing skills and diagnostics, with pre-minors that preview year three. In year three you choose a learning line: Clinical, Psychopathology, Health and Prevention, Social and Organisational Psychology, or Genes, Cognition and Behaviour. You also take a minor and write an independent bachelor's thesis.

name: Animal Sciences
overview: Year one covers animal biology, the diversity of domesticated animals, chemistry, mathematics and statistics, and includes an internship. Year two brings genetics, ecology, immunology, zoology, animal nutrition and epidemiology, and you choose between Animal Management and Care, which looks at animals and their effects on environment and society, and Biological Functioning of Animals, which looks at internal processes. Teaching mixes lectures, group tutorials, lab and computer practicals, excursions and fieldwork. Year three offers electives and a minor, possibly abroad, and an original research thesis. Graduates work as policy advisers, researchers, teachers and animal welfare inspectors, often after a master's in animal sciences.

name: Data Science for Global Challenges
overview: Year one combines life sciences, mathematics, statistics and computer science, and applies data science to global challenges. Year two moves to advanced data science and artificial intelligence techniques, with an emphasis on using them responsibly. You learn programming, statistical analysis and model building, and work with diverse data including satellite and sensor data, in group work that builds interdisciplinary collaboration. In year three you take electives or a minor, at one of nearly 50 options or another university, and finish with a capstone project applying data science to a global challenge. Graduates work as data scientists, AI and geo-data specialists, or epidemiologists.

name: Earth System Sciences
overview: Year one covers the core theories of the Earth system, from processes underground to the atmosphere, with fieldwork and lab experience. Year two turns to landscape formation, water quality, weather and climate, and environmental and climate modelling, with field excursions. Teaching mixes lectures, practicals, outdoor measurements, lab experiments, data analysis and computer simulation. In year three you take a minor in the Netherlands or abroad, such as Disaster and Risk Resilience, then deepen one domain, soil, water or atmosphere, or all three, in an individual research project. Graduates work as climate researchers, water managers and environmental advisors, for example at KNMI or Deltares.

name: Environmental Sciences
overview: Year one covers mathematics, statistics and chemistry together with soil processes, water systems and environmental technology, applied to real sustainability challenges. In year two you prepare for and then choose a specialisation: technological, social or systems-oriented environmental science. Teaching includes lectures, group work, lab practicals, computer simulations and fieldwork, with more support staff than is typical at Dutch universities. In year three you complete your specialisation, take electives or a self-designed set of courses, and a minor such as geo-information or ecosystem governance, and finish with an independent research thesis. Graduates work as environmental researchers, policy advisers and sustainability managers.

name: Food Technology
overview: Year one covers mathematics, chemistry, biology, physics, microbiology and toxicology, and an introduction to food technology with excursions. Year two applies these to food microbiology, chemistry, preservation, engineering, food hazards, packaging design and quality systems, and you develop your own food product. Teaching uses lectures, tutorials, project-based learning and practicals. In year three you have free electives, case studies on real industry problems and an independent graduation thesis, with minors such as Foods of Animal Origin, an internship or study abroad. Graduates work as product developers, R&D specialists and quality managers at companies like Unilever and Heineken.

name: International Land and Water Management
overview: Year one covers soil and water, agronomy, sociology, economics and hydraulics, with a case study and fieldwork in the Netherlands. Year two looks at the engineering, socio-economic and policy sides of land and water management, with an excursion to southern Europe to study irrigation and erosion control. Teaching uses lectures, tutorials, computer-based learning and fieldwork, with small-group work on real cases. In year three you do a practical internship abroad, take electives or a minor such as Climate Change, GIS or Education, and write a final research thesis. Graduates work as consultants, project managers and policy officers.

name: Marine Sciences
overview: Year one analyses diverse marine systems and teaches research methods across disciplines, ending in fieldwork on the Wadden Sea and North Sea. Year two focuses on nature-inspired solutions to international challenges, including the responsible use of generative AI, and you present findings to industry professionals. Teaching combines lectures, group projects, lab and computer practicals and excursions to marine research institutes and coastal sites such as Texel and Croatia. In year three an elective semester allows a minor, for example Seagriculture, followed by a final project with graduation research on nature-based solutions. Graduates work as marine researchers and fisheries or aquaculture managers.

name: Tourism (joint degree)
overview: Year one covers tourism, sociology, economics, environmental sciences and research methods, ending in a National Field Practicum in the Netherlands. Year two adds development, intercultural studies, landscape planning and environmental systems analysis, with tourism simulations and an international field practicum. Teaching is lectures and problem-based tutorials in which a group and a supervisor solve a case. Year three offers electives, then specialisations such as risk communication or community development, and a bachelor's thesis. The degree is taught jointly with Breda University of Applied Sciences, and graduates work as junior strategists, marketers and researchers.

name: Communication and Information Studies
overview: You study how communication works and what role language plays in it, choosing a track from year one; the English-taught tracks are Language and Media and Applied Linguistics. Language and Media covers discourse analysis, global English, multilingual communication in the EU, visual design, language policy in organisations and how organisations use media with business and consumers. Applied Linguistics covers language structure, child language acquisition, language disorders, multilingualism and the role of large language models. Year three offers a minor or an internship, then social media analytics and a bachelor's thesis based on your own research. The small scale gives plenty of contact with lecturers.
